design_detail: Cross-sectional PET study with [11C]WIN-35,428 (2-β-carbomethoxy-3β-(4-[11C]fluorophenyl)tropane) in 11 men who had used only methamphetamine and 9 men who had not, at one Japanese centre. Dopamine transporter binding potential (k3/k4, three-compartment four-parameter model, arterial input function, cerebellar cortex as the reference for K1/k2) was measured in the caudate/putamen, nucleus accumbens and prefrontal cortex and correlated, within the methamphetamine group only, with duration of use, duration of abstinence, Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS) scores and a craving score.
can_establish: That in this small sample, men abstinent from methamphetamine (7 days to 1.5 years) had lower dopamine transporter binding potential in all three regions than men who had not used it, and that within the methamphetamine group lower striatal and accumbens binding went with longer reported use and higher ratings of positive psychiatric symptoms.
cannot_establish: That methamphetamine caused the lower binding (no pre-use scan, no dose data, and the psychiatric symptoms that brought most participants into care could themselves mark a pre-existing difference; the authors concede this on p. 1213); that the lower binding means lost dopamine terminals rather than reduced transporter expression; that the reduction is lasting (the null correlation with abstinence rests on 11 people); or the direction of the symptom association in time.

sample.recruitment: The methamphetamine group was referred from three Japanese psychiatric services (Hamamatsu University Hospital, Seimei Hospital, Hattori Mental Hospital); how the comparison group was recruited is not stated (p. 1207).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: All participants men, with no parkinsonism or other neurological abnormality and no history of seizures, dyskinesia or coma. Nicotine, alcohol and other drug use screened with the SCID (non-patient version): no participant met nicotine or alcohol abuse criteria; the methamphetamine group had used no drug other than methamphetamine and the comparison group no drug at all. The comparison group had no psychiatric disorder, including substance use disorders, on the SCID (p. 1207).
sample.demographics: Methamphetamine group: 11 men, mean age 27.4 years (SD 5.6), education 11.5 years (SD 1.2). Comparison group: 9 men, mean age 26.9 (SD 4.5), education 11.8 (SD 0.7). Age and education did not differ significantly (pp. 1207–1208). Individual ages, durations of use (1 month to 15 years), abstinence (7 days to 1.5 years) and route (7 intravenous, 4 smoked) are in Table 1 (p. 1207).
sample.attrition: Not applicable; single scan, no follow-up.
sample.selection_effects: A clinically selected group: participants were referred from psychiatric services and 8 of 11 had previously experienced methamphetamine psychosis, so the sample is weighted towards people with psychiatric consequences of use, not towards people who use methamphetamine generally. The comparison group's source is not stated, and whether the two groups came from comparable populations cannot be checked. Only men were studied.

exposure.measurement: Self-report corroborated by interviews with family members and by medical records; recent use excluded by urine drug screening, including on the day of the scan (p. 1207; p. 1212).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Duration of use only, defined as the interval between first and last use with abstinence periods longer than 1 month subtracted: 1 month to 15 years (Table 1, p. 1207). Route as reported: intravenous in 7, smoked in 4 (Table 1 footnotes, p. 1207). No dose, frequency or cumulative amount was measured anywhere in the paper, although the discussion states that participants used methamphetamine recreationally and had no history of high-dose use (p. 1211).
exposure.polysubstance: By design, people who used any drug other than methamphetamine were excluded, and the comparison group had used no drug; both groups were described as occasional smokers and drinkers who met no nicotine or alcohol abuse criterion (p. 1207). This is the study's main strength over earlier PET work, in which other drug use was present or unknown (p. 1210).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: 7 days to 1.5 years (Table 1, p. 1207), verified by regular urine drug screens including one on the scan day (p. 1212). Four participants had received neuroleptics previously (last exposure 1 week to 1 year before); none was taking them at the scan (p. 1208).

comparison.controls: 9 men with no history of psychiatric disorder, substance use disorder or any illicit drug use (SCID), scanned with the same tracer and scanner (p. 1207).
comparison.matching: Selected to be similar in age and education; no formal matching procedure, covariate adjustment or sex comparison is described, and no comparison of smoking or drinking quantity is given beyond the statement of similar occasional habits (p. 1207).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use scan, no premorbid IQ or psychiatric baseline. The authors note that the methamphetamine group had no psychotic symptoms before use (from interview and records), but a pre-existing difference in transporter density cannot be excluded and they say so (p. 1213).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: None reported: the comparison group had no experience of any other drug and occasional alcohol and tobacco use only (p. 1207).

outcomes.instruments: PET (SHR2400 scanner) with [11C]WIN-35,428, 450 MBq bolus, 38 frames over 90 minutes, arterial sampling with metabolite correction; regions of interest drawn by hand on the PET display, with the corresponding 0.3 T MRI images referred to as anatomical landmarks (the paper does not describe co-registration); dopamine transporter binding potential expressed as k3/k4 (p. 1207). Symptoms: BPRS total and the positive- and negative-symptom subscales, rated by one trained psychiatrist blind to the PET data; craving on a 0–5 scale adapted from the Subjective Craving Scale for Alcohol Dependence (p. 1207).
outcomes.validity_norms: No normative data for binding potential; comparison is with the 9 scanned men. The craving scale was adapted from an alcohol instrument and no validation for methamphetamine is given.
outcomes.operationalization: Transporter 'reduction' is the group difference in mean binding potential; 'persistent psychiatric symptoms' are BPRS ratings on the scan day in people abstinent at least 7 days, with recent use excluded by urine screen (pp. 1207, 1212).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Statistical significance was set at p<0.05 for all tests (p. 1207): three group comparisons of binding potential, thirteen reported rank correlations and five prefrontal correlations reported only as absent ('data not shown', p. 1209); the Methods also describe group comparisons of K1, k2, k3, k4 and K1/k2 whose results are not reported.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Partial and stated in both directions: the closing sentence of the PET paragraph says the procedure (region drawing and binding-potential calculation, which share one paragraph) was done blind to the clinical data, and the BPRS was rated blind to the PET data by the first author (Y.S., p. 1207). Blinding to group membership is not stated, and who collected the use histories, and whether the BPRS rater knew them, is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: Binding potential (k3/k4), comparison group vs methamphetamine group: caudate/putamen 4.40 (SD 0.18) vs 3.51 (SD 0.45), 20.2% lower; nucleus accumbens 4.16 (SD 0.64) vs 2.93 (SD 0.77), 29.6% lower; prefrontal cortex 0.18 (SD 0.05) vs 0.12 (SD 0.03), 33.3% lower (pp. 1208–1209). Mann-Whitney U: caudate/putamen U=1.0, N=20, p<0.001; nucleus accumbens U=8.5, N=20, p<0.001; prefrontal cortex U=23.5, N=20, p<0.05 (p. 1209). No confidence intervals are given. Editors' calculation from the printed means and SDs (Hedges' g, pooled SD, approximate because the groups are small and the distributions are not described): caudate/putamen about 2.4, nucleus accumbens about 1.6, prefrontal cortex about 1.4; the intervals around these values are wide with 11 and 9 participants. Correlations are Kendall's tau within the methamphetamine group (n=11).
analysis.covariates: None. Unadjusted rank tests throughout; age, education, duration of use, route, prior neuroleptic exposure and abstinence were not entered into any model.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned (the study predates trial-registry practice for such work).
analysis.selective_reporting: Prefrontal correlations are reported only as 'data not shown' (p. 1209), and the group comparisons of the individual rate constants described in the Methods are not reported. The craving-scale correlations are given with statistics only where significant; the non-significant ones are described in words (p. 1209).
analysis.power: Not reported; no sample-size calculation. With 11 and 9 participants only large differences could be detected, and the rank correlations in 11 people have very wide intervals (a Kendall tau of −0.48 in n=11 is at the edge of significance).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 11 men abstinent from methamphetamine and 9 men who had not used it, dopamine transporter binding potential was lower in the caudate/putamen (20.2%), nucleus accumbens (29.6%) and prefrontal cortex (33.3%). Within the methamphetamine group, lower caudate/putamen and accumbens binding went with longer reported duration of use and with higher BPRS positive-symptom scores, and the duration of use itself correlated with positive symptoms; binding did not correlate with how long people had been abstinent, and craving correlated only with abstinence duration.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that "longer use of methamphetamine may cause more severe psychiatric symptoms" and greater transporter reduction, that the reduction "may be long-lasting" after use stops, and that persistent psychiatric symptoms may be attributable to it (p. 1206); the discussion states that longer use induces greater reduction, which in turn is associated with more residual symptoms (p. 1212). Three gaps: (1) causal and temporal language from one cross-sectional scan per person, in a sample selected through psychiatric services; (2) the persistence claim rests on a non-significant correlation with abstinence duration in 11 people, which is absence of evidence rather than evidence of persistence, and the authors' support for it is a previous study rather than their own data (p. 1212); (3) duration of use is treated as a proxy for cumulative dose (pp. 1211–1212) although no dose, frequency or amount was measured, and the statement that nobody had used high doses has no measurement behind it. The paper's own closing caveat, that pre-existing transporter reduction cannot be ruled out, is stated only on p. 1213 and does not reach the abstract.

timeline.event: PET with the same tracer in 6 people abstinent from methamphetamine or methcathinone: caudate and putamen binding 23–25% lower than in 10 controls, but all participants reported other illicit drug use
PET with [11C]d-threo-methylphenidate in 15 people with methamphetamine dependence: caudate 27.8% and putamen 21.1% lower than 18 controls, with other drug use not quantified

The same Hamamatsu group reported transporter reductions with longer-lasting psychiatric symptoms in a larger sample (Sekine et al., 2003), which shares investigators and site and is therefore not an independent replication
Critical review summarizing this study as about 20% lower striatal binding in people without other illicit drug use, while noting that the imaging difference has no established functional meaning
Critical assessment of whether lower transporter binding in people who use methamphetamine indicates damage to dopamine neurons

replication.where_it_stands: The direction (lower striatal transporter binding) is consistent across independent groups, tracers and post-mortem tissue. This study adds the strongest available control for polysubstance use, and extends the finding to the nucleus accumbens and prefrontal cortex, but with 11 and 9 men and no dose data. Whether the difference reflects lost terminals, transporter regulation or a pre-existing trait, and whether it recovers, remain open.

funding.funder: Scientific Research grant from the Ministry of Health and Welfare of Japan and a Target-Oriented Research and Development grant from the Ministry of Science and Technology of Japan (p. 1213).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: the article carries no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: At least one author is from the Central Research Laboratory of Hamamatsu Photonics K.K., the company that made the PET scanner and is credited with it in the Methods; the affiliation note lists three institutions without saying which authors belong to which, so the number of authors from the company cannot be checked from the PDF (pp. 1207, 1213). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study with transporter imaging before and after the onset of regular use (or a discordant-sibling or twin design) in people without other drug use, with a transporter-independent terminal marker such as VMAT2 measured in the same people, blinded symptom ratings at several time points, and measured dose rather than duration as the exposure.

domains.note: No adjustment of any kind. Groups are small and the methamphetamine group differs in psychiatric status by selection; prior neuroleptic exposure in 4 participants is dismissed by citation rather than modelled; no dose data; age and education similar but unadjusted.

Duration of use comes from self-report corroborated by family and records, which is better than self-report alone, but dose, frequency and purity are absent, so 'longer use' cannot be read as 'more drug'. Abstinence is urine-verified.

Referred from three psychiatric services, with 8 of 11 having had methamphetamine psychosis, against a comparison group of unstated origin; the symptom–transporter correlation is estimated inside this selected group.
Four participants had received neuroleptics (up to a year before the scan); abstinence ranged from 7 days to 1.5 years, so time since use varies by a factor of about 80 across the group.
All 20 participants contributed scans and all 11 in the methamphetamine group contributed clinical ratings.

Binding potential is quantified with arterial input and metabolite correction and computed blind to clinical data, and the BPRS was rated blind to the PET data; but regions were drawn by hand and the prefrontal binding potential (0.12–0.18) is close to the tracer's non-specific floor, as the authors themselves note in calling for a tracer with a higher specific-to-nonspecific ratio (p. 1211).
Twenty-one or more tests at p<0.05 with no correction; prefrontal correlations and the rate-constant comparisons are reported only as absent or not at all.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The group difference in transporter binding is large and measured with a quantitative method applied blind to clinical data, and the exclusion of other drug use removes a confounder that weakens most comparable studies. But the methamphetamine group was recruited through psychiatric services and most had had psychosis, there is no dose measurement, nothing is adjusted, and the symptom and duration correlations come from 11 people with no correction for multiplicity. The source can be cited for the direction and approximate size of the group difference in people without other illicit drug use, and for the existence of a within-group association between transporter binding and positive symptoms; it cannot be cited for causation, for persistence after abstinence, or for a dose–response relationship.

key_findings.finding: Dopamine transporter binding potential (k3/k4) in the caudate/putamen was 4.40 (SD 0.18) in the 9 men of the comparison group and 3.51 (SD 0.45) in the 11 men of the methamphetamine group, 20.2% lower.
key_findings.locator: Results, last paragraph of p. 1208 continuing on p. 1209 (right column of p. 1208); Figure 4 (p. 1210)

key_findings.finding: In the nucleus accumbens the binding potentials were 4.16 (SD 0.64) and 2.93 (SD 0.77), 29.6% lower; in the prefrontal cortex 0.18 (SD 0.05) and 0.12 (SD 0.03), 33.3% lower.
key_findings.note: The prefrontal values are an order of magnitude smaller than the striatal ones and, in the editors' reading, close to the tracer's non-specific binding (the paper does not say so); the authors call for a tracer with a higher specific-to-nonspecific ratio before prefrontal conclusions are drawn (p. 1211).

key_findings.finding: All three regional differences were significant on the Mann-Whitney U test: caudate/putamen U=1.0, N=20, p<0.001; nucleus accumbens U=8.5, N=20, p<0.001; prefrontal cortex U=23.5, N=20, p<0.05.
Within the methamphetamine group (n=11), binding potential fell as reported duration of use rose: caudate/putamen Kendall's tau −0.48 (p<0.05), nucleus accumbens tau −0.73 (p<0.01).
key_findings.note: Duration of use, not dose: no quantity of drug was measured anywhere in the study.

key_findings.finding: Binding potential did not correlate with duration of abstinence (7 days to 1.5 years) in either the caudate/putamen or the nucleus accumbens.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (left column, continuing right column); Figure 5 (p. 1211)
key_findings.note: A non-significant correlation in 11 people; the discussion nonetheless reads it as evidence that the reduction is long-lasting (p. 1212).

key_findings.finding: Caudate/putamen binding correlated negatively with the BPRS total score (tau −0.62, p<0.05); the nucleus accumbens did not. Both regions correlated negatively with the BPRS positive-symptom subscale (caudate/putamen tau −0.73, p<0.01; nucleus accumbens tau −0.50, p<0.05).

The BPRS positive-symptom score rose with duration of methamphetamine use (tau 0.64, p<0.01), and the craving score fell as abstinence lengthened (tau −0.50, p<0.05) but was unrelated to duration of use and to binding potential in either region.
No correlation was found between prefrontal cortex binding and any clinical measure; these analyses are reported only as 'data not shown'.

Eight of the 11 men in the methamphetamine group had previously experienced methamphetamine psychosis. In the 2 weeks before the scan, 3 had no psychiatric symptoms, 4 had persistent anxiety-like but not psychotic symptoms and 3 had persistent psychotic symptoms; a further man (participant 1), whose psychotic symptoms began during use, still had them on the scan day, so 4 of the 11 had psychotic symptoms at the scan. None had a history of psychotic symptoms before methamphetamine use, none showed negative symptoms at the examination, and none was taking neuroleptics, although 4 had received them earlier.

Participants used only methamphetamine: the SCID excluded any other illicit drug use in the methamphetamine group and any illicit drug use in the comparison group, and neither group met nicotine or alcohol abuse criteria.

The reduction here (about 20% in the caudate/putamen) is compared by the authors with about 80% striatal transporter loss measured with the same scanner and tracer in unmedicated Parkinson's disease; no participants with Parkinson's disease were studied here.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph beginning 'In a previous study using the same PET scanner'

key_findings.finding: Duration of use was defined as the interval between first and last use with abstinence periods longer than one month subtracted, and ranged from 1 month to 15 years; 7 participants had used methamphetamine intravenously and 4 by smoking.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 and its footnotes; Method › Subjects, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: No participant had a history of seizures, dyskinesia or coma, complications the authors link to intoxication with high-dose methamphetamine; all were men without signs of parkinsonism or other neurological abnormality. The paper does not say whether this was an exclusion rule or a description of the group.
key_findings.note: If it was an exclusion rule, the most severe cases are absent from the methamphetamine group (editors' reading), which bears on how far the 20–33% reductions generalize.

reporting_issues.issue: Every Kendall's tau is reported with 'df=10'. A rank correlation has no degrees of freedom, and for n=11 the conventional correlation degrees of freedom would be n−2=9; the printed df appears to be n−1.
reporting_issues.consequence: The p-values can be approximately reconstructed from tau and n = 11 (editors' calculation, normal approximation without tie correction: tau −0.48 gives p of about 0.04, −0.50 about 0.03, −0.62 about 0.008, 0.64 about 0.006 and −0.73 about 0.002), so the printed thresholds are consistent and only the df label is non-standard; a tau of −0.48 is still near the significance boundary, so the exact test would matter for the weaker correlations.

reporting_issues.issue: The mean age printed for the methamphetamine group (27.4 years, SD 5.6) does not match the ages listed for the same 11 participants in Table 1, which give a mean of 28.0 and an SD of 5.7 (editors' calculation from the eleven values).
reporting_issues.consequence: Small, but it shows that the demographic text and Table 1 were not reconciled; the age comparison between groups is unaffected in substance.

reporting_issues.issue: Duration of use is treated in the discussion as a proxy for cumulative dose ('the duration of methamphetamine use ... may represent this dose dependency'), and the claim that nobody had used high doses is made in the same paragraph, although no dose, frequency or amount was measured in the study.
reporting_issues.consequence: The dose–response reading of the duration correlation is unsupported by any measured exposure quantity; the correlation can only be read as with time since first use.

reporting_issues.issue: Twenty-one or more statistical tests are reported at an uncorrected p<0.05, and the prefrontal correlations are reported only as 'data not shown'.
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one of the weaker significant correlations (tau around −0.48 to −0.50) would be expected by chance; the absent prefrontal results cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that the transporter reduction was significantly associated with the duration of use and closely related to the severity of persistent psychiatric symptoms, without saying that both associations are rank correlations inside a group of 11 people drawn from psychiatric services.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader who stops at the abstract will take a within-group correlation in 11 people for an established dose–symptom relationship.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion suggests that methamphetamine causes a reduction of transporter density in the human brain, qualified only by the small number of participants (p. 1210), and says that the small caudate/putamen reduction appears to have predictive value for psychiatric signs and that people who use methamphetamine may have a greater risk of Parkinson's disease as they age (p. 1212), although each person was scanned once, nobody was followed and nobody was assessed for Parkinson's disease beyond the exclusion of signs of parkinsonism.
reporting_issues.consequence: The causal, predictive and Parkinson's-disease-risk readings go beyond a cross-sectional comparison of 11 and 9 men, and the authors' own caveat that a pre-existing reduction cannot be ruled out (p. 1213) does not reach these sentences.

reporting_issues.issue: The BPRS was rated by a research psychiatrist identified only by initials (Y.S., the first author), stated to be blind to the PET data; who collected the use histories is not stated and blinding to them is not claimed.
reporting_issues.consequence: The correlation of positive-symptom scores with duration of use (tau 0.64) is not shown to have been rated blind to duration, and the rater is also an author.

disagreements.reviewer: Reader 10 (corrected): the discussion's reading of the null correlation (a lasting reduction could occur, supported by a previous PET study) is on p. 1212, in the paragraph beginning with the null correlation, not on p. 1211.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed on the layout of p. 1212 (left column): the paragraph on duration of abstinence is there; p. 1211 ends in the middle of the dose-dependency sentence. Page corrected in the note.

disagreements.resolution: Confirmed on the layout of pp. 1211-1212: the dose-dependency sentence breaks across the two pages. Page corrected in point 3 of the claimed text.

disagreements.first_pass: Eight of the 11 men in the methamphetamine group had previously experienced methamphetamine psychosis; at the scan, 3 had persistent psychotic symptoms, 4 had persistent anxiety-like symptoms and 3 had none; none had a psychiatric history predating methamphetamine use, and none was taking neuroleptics, although 4 had received them earlier.
disagreements.reviewer: Reader 10 (corrected): (a) the symptom counts describe the 2 weeks before the PET examination: 3 with persistent psychotic symptoms, 4 with anxiety-like symptoms and 3 with none, plus participant 1, whose psychotic symptoms began during use and were still present on the scan day (7 days abstinent), so 4 of 11 had psychotic symptoms at the scan; (b) the paper says none had a history of psychotic symptoms before methamphetamine use, not that none had any psychiatric history (p. 1208, Results, 1st paragraph).
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed on p. 1208 (Results, 1st paragraph) and Table 1 (participant 1: 7 days abstinent, auditory hallucinations). Finding rewritten with the 2-week window, participant 1, and the exact history wording.

disagreements.first_pass: The test statistics cannot be reconstructed from what is printed; with n=11 a tau of −0.48 is near the significance boundary, so the exact test matters for the weaker correlations.
disagreements.reviewer: Reader 10 (corrected): the issue stands (df = 10 is a non-standard label), but the consequence should be withdrawn because the p-values can be approximately reconstructed from tau and n = 11 (tau -0.48 gives p of about 0.04; -0.50, 0.03; -0.62, 0.008; 0.64, 0.006; -0.73, 0.002).
disagreements.resolution: Recomputed with the normal approximation for Kendall's tau (z = 3 tau sqrt(n(n-1)) / sqrt(2(2n+5)), n = 11): p = 0.040, 0.032, 0.008, 0.006 and 0.002; all consistent with the printed thresholds. The claim that the statistics cannot be reconstructed is withdrawn; the issue text is unchanged.
